description: Detailed host metrics for the Windows machine. Built against the 152 metrics this exporter actually publishes, from the eight default collectors: cpu, memory, logical_disk, physical_disk, net, os, service, system. Pagefile size and pending updates are not available without enabling further collectors.

panels.description: Red below 1 hour, amber below 1 day. This host has a history of unexpected reboots, so a short uptime is a signal rather than noise.
panels.title: Uptime

panels.description: Cross-check against Event 41 entries in the Windows system log.
panels.title: Last boot

panels.description: Sanity check. Expect about 16 GiB.
panels.title: Physical memory

panels.description: Needed to read the processor queue length correctly.
panels.title: Logical processors

panels.description: A runaway process count is an early warning. The limit is windows_system_processes_limit.
panels.title: Processes

panels.description: Threads waiting for a core. The Windows equivalent of load average. Compare against the core count.
panels.title: Processor queue

panels.description: Build and version strings from the os collector.
panels.title: Windows version

panels.description: High context switching with low CPU usually means too many threads competing for cores.
panels.title: Threads and context switches

panels.description: Busy is 100 minus idle. Same shape as the Mac query, different metric name. That divergence is why recording rules exist.
panels.title: CPU busy

panels.description: Windows modes are user, privileged, interrupt and dpc. Privileged is kernel time; there is no iowait.
panels.title: CPU by mode

panels.description: The label is core, not cpu as on Linux and macOS. Spots a single pinned core.
panels.title: CPU per core

panels.description: A spike in deferred procedure calls points at a driver. A plausible lead for the Event 41 crashes on this host, which leave no dump.
panels.title: Interrupts and DPCs

panels.description: Thermal or power throttling shows here before it shows as slowness.
panels.title: Core frequency

panels.description: Actual delivered performance against nominal. Diverges from frequency under turbo or throttling.
panels.title: Processor performance

panels.description: Available is the honest Windows figure. This gauge is meaningful here in a way the macOS equivalent is not, because macOS free excludes cache.
panels.title: Memory used

panels.description: Available includes reclaimable standby cache. Free does not, which is why the two differ.
panels.title: Available and total

panels.description: Committed approaching the limit means allocations start failing. A different failure from running out of physical RAM.
panels.title: Committed memory

panels.description: The closest thing this build has to a pagefile usage gauge, since no pagefile metrics are exported.
panels.title: Commit charge used

panels.description: Standby cache is reclaimable. Counting it as used overstates memory pressure.
panels.title: Cache and standby

panels.description: Steadily growing nonpaged pool is a classic driver memory leak, and another candidate cause for an unexplained hang.
panels.title: Pool memory

panels.description: Soft faults are normal and cheap. Judge pressure by the paging panel below, not by this one alone.
panels.title: Page faults

panels.description: Exhaustion causes allocation failures that look like random application crashes.
panels.title: Free system page table entries

panels.description: Sustained page reads are the clearest sign of genuine memory pressure. These are hard faults served from disk.
panels.title: Paging activity

panels.description: Pages rather than operations. The ratio against the panel to the left shows how many pages each operation moves.
panels.title: Pages read and written

panels.description: Pagefile SIZE is not available: this build has no pagefile collector enabled. Reinstall with ENABLED_COLLECTORS including pagefile to get it. Use commit charge as a proxy meanwhile.
panels.title: Total paging operations

panels.description: Every volume. 85 matches the WindowsDiskFilling alert threshold, so dashboard and alert agree.
panels.title: Disk used percent

panels.description: Thresholds are 20 GiB and 50 GiB, matching the Mac dashboard.
panels.title: Free space by volume

panels.description: Negative means filling. Needs 6h of history, which current retention only just provides.
panels.title: Days until C: is full

panels.description: Per logical volume.
panels.title: Throughput

panels.description: Operations per second. Throughput and IOPS tell different stories about the same workload.
panels.title: IOPS

panels.description: Average seconds per operation. Rising latency at flat throughput means the device is struggling, which is a hardware signal.
panels.title: Latency per operation

panels.description: A sustained queue means the disk cannot keep up with demand.
panels.title: Queue length

panels.description: Low idle time is how Windows expresses a saturated disk.
panels.title: Idle percent

panels.description: Requests split because the data was not contiguous. A fragmentation signal.
panels.title: Split IO

panels.description: Per physical device rather than per volume. The two differ when volumes share a device.
panels.title: Physical throughput

panels.description: Device level latency. Closer to the hardware than the logical volume view, so better evidence of a failing drive.
panels.title: Physical latency

panels.description: Queue rising while idle falls is a saturated device.
panels.title: Physical queue and idle

panels.description: The nic label carries the full adapter name. Expect several virtual adapters alongside the Wi-Fi one.
panels.title: Throughput

panels.description: Packet rate and byte rate diverge when packet sizes change.
panels.title: Packets per second

panels.description: This host is on Wi-Fi, where sustained errors point at interference or a driver. Relevant given the ICMP flapping already observed on this network.
panels.title: Errors and discards, last 1h

panels.description: The exporter reports bandwidth in BYTES per second, so this multiplies by 8 to show bits. A Wi-Fi adapter renegotiating down looks like a server problem from the other end.
panels.title: Link speed and output queue

panels.description: Which adapters are actually up. 1 means operational.
panels.title: Adapter status

panels.description: The exporter reporting on itself. If the service stops this goes to No data rather than 0, which is why the TargetDown alert matters too.
panels.title: windows_exporter running

panels.description: Total count. A sharp drop is worth investigating.
panels.title: Services running

panels.description: Services that should be running and are not. Far more actionable than a raw stopped count.
panels.title: Auto-start services stopped

panels.description: The exporter can report up while one collector silently fails, leaving this row empty.
panels.title: Service collector health

panels.description: The actionable list. Empty is good.
panels.title: Stopped auto-start services

panels.description: 1 means the collector ran. 0 explains an empty panel elsewhere on this dashboard.
panels.title: Collectors

panels.description: A slow collector lengthens every scrape. The service collector is usually the slowest.
panels.title: Collector duration

panels.description: A timing-out collector drops its metrics without the exporter appearing down.
panels.title: Collector timeouts and scrape duration

title: Windows host detail
